chain.kicker: Where this page is, and why a page like this exists here
chain.p1: Robinhood Chain is an Arbitrum Orbit network. It runs the Nitro execution engine, settles to Ethereum and posts its data there in blobs, which is the same shape Arbitrum One has. Gas is paid in ETH; there is no separate gas token to hold first. Every Ethereum wallet and every EVM tool works against it without a change, which is why a launch here costs almost nothing to make.
chain.p2: The explorer for this chain is Blockscout, at robinhoodchain.blockscout.com. Etherscan does not index it. A link that claims to show you a launch on this chain through Etherscan is showing you a different chain, or nothing.
chain.p3: A busy network attracts copies of itself, and this one has them: lookalike explorers, lookalike endpoints, lookalike front ends. The same instinct runs one level down, into the launches themselves. A name that is almost a name you know. A ticker that is almost a ticker you know. Five links that are almost the right five. That is the whole reason this page reads strings, and the whole reason it refuses to tell you what they mean.
reads.p1: This page reads seven strings a launch publishes about itself and compares each with the same string on every launch of one day. It does not open the contract, price anything or resolve an address. Every comparison is on normalized text: trimmed, lowercased where case carries no meaning, and folded where the alias table says two spellings name one resource.
reads.N1: the ticker after normalization, against every ticker in the window.
reads.N2: the name after normalization, against every name in the window.
reads.N3: the ticker and the name folded to a skeleton, against every skeleton in the window; reported only when the group holds more than one spelling.
reads.I1: each of the five link fields, folded through the alias table, against every link in the window.
reads.I2: the logo URI as written, against every logo in the window.
reads.I3: the creator fee recipient as text, against every recipient in the window; reported only when different deployers carry it.
reads.I4: the description, at {min_words} words or more, against every description in the window.
reads.p2: Each row says whether the value is shared, with how many launches, from how many deployers, and since when. That is the whole output.
definitions.shared.d: the same value, after normalization, appears on other launches in the window
definitions.lookalike.d: different spellings that fold to one shape under the skeleton table; a value spelled identically is shared, not a lookalike
definitions.deployer.d: the address that appears as the deployer in the factory record
definitions.window.d: one day, block range and both timestamps stated below
definitions.carry.d: the count includes every launch in the window that has the value, which may include the one you pasted
definitions.close: None of this predicts anything. A shared ticker is a fact about strings, not a signal about a launch.
reproduce.p1: The index is built from one pass over the launch log of the window above, one multicall per token, against the public RPC, with no key. Anyone can rebuild it from the same block window and compare the hash.
reproduce.p2: The command re-runs the collector over the window recorded in the numbers file, rebuilds the index, and prints both hashes and whether they match. A rerun can differ if the endpoint returns differently under load; the shipped index is the one whose hash is printed here.
run.p1: Everything on this page can be run on your own machine. The repository needs Node and nothing else: no runtime dependency, nothing to install beyond the clone. The tests check the vendor table against every copied file, the token block in its three states, the engine, the ABI, the gate and the index schema. The build writes this page from the templates, the numbers file and the index, and refuses a digit that did not arrive by substitution.
run.p2: The last command is the one that produced the hash printed above. It re-runs the collector over the recorded window against the public RPC, rebuilds the index in a temporary directory, and prints both hashes and whether they match.
run.test: the vendor table, the engine, the schema, the token states
run.build: the page, from the templates and the index
run.verify: rebuild the index from the same window, compare the hash
run.kicker: Node and nothing else. No key, no account, no install beyond the clone
run.c1.p: clone it, read it, change it
run.c2.p: the same page you are reading, built from the templates and the index
run.c3.p: rebuilt from the same block window, hash printed and compared
run.wide.p: Nothing here needs a key. The tests read the tree only. The build reads the templates, the numbers file and the index and writes one page. Only the last command goes to the network, and it goes to the same public endpoint the collector uses, with no key and the same limiter.
origin.p1: This is the second site of lintcha. The first reads the text people put in AI bot profiles: the charter a bot publishes about itself, checked against a corpus of such charters, with no score.
origin.p2: The same method is pointed here at token launches, because both are text written once, copied widely, and never read again: a name, a ticker, a description, a few links, set at launch and left as they are. Both sites read that text and stop.
origin.p3: The engine, the skeleton table, the alias table and the tests are written in lintcha and copied here unchanged; the index is built here, from this chain's launch log, on its own schedule.
method.p1: This section states what the collector read, how each field is normalized before it is hashed, the two tables that fold spellings and hosts, the floor under every count, and what the index holds. The tables are written from the engine's own files at build time, so they cannot drift from the code that runs in your browser.
method.window.p: One day: the {hours} hours ending at the latest finalised block at the time of the run, found by bisecting block timestamps, so the window is stated as a block range and two UTC timestamps, {from_stamp} to {to_stamp}. A day is what one pass over the launch log covers at the pace the public endpoint sustains without a key; a longer window would say more about strings and nothing more about launches.
method.collector.p: One pass over the launch log of the pons factory on Robinhood Chain over that block range; then, per token, the name, the ticker and the token record through one multicall, the creator fee recipient from the factory's own record, and the block dates. Every field is normalized with the same engine this page runs, hashed, and counted per namespace with the number of distinct deployers and the first date. Addresses and raw strings live in that process's memory only; what it writes is counted hashes and the run's own figures, the ones printed in section eight.
method.norm.link_raw.v: NFC, whitespace collapsed. For a web address, with http, https or no scheme: the scheme dropped, the host lowercased, a leading {code}www.{/code}, trailing slashes and the fragment removed; the path keeps its case. Any other scheme is kept whole, whitespace collapsed only.
method.norm.link_folded.v: The raw form, then the alias table below. A bare handle in a field that names its platform becomes that platform's page; a host in the table is replaced by the host it stands for and its path lowercased. Shorteners and redirects never fold: expanding one is a network call, and the page makes none.
method.norm.logo.v: The raw link form, never folded. Nothing is resolved or fetched.
method.norm.recipient.v: Whitespace collapsed, lowercased, matched against {code}{recipient_pattern}{/code}; checksum case is cosmetic. The zero address counts as empty; anything else that fails the pattern is not readable.
method.norm.description.v: NFKC, lowercased, web addresses stripped, apostrophes removed without a space so a contraction stays one word, everything that is not a letter, a number or whitespace replaced by a space, whitespace collapsed. Compared at {min_words} words or more; under that it is too short to compare.
method.norm.ticker.v: NFC, whitespace collapsed, leading dollar signs and whitespace stripped, uppercased.
method.norm.name.v: NFKC, lowercased, punctuation removed, whitespace collapsed.
method.norm.skeleton.v: Lowercased, NFKD, marks removed, the character table applied one character at a time, then the pairs folded left to right. Two strings that differ as strings and agree as skeletons are a lookalike.
method.floor.p: An entry is kept when {count_floor} launches or more carry the value, so absence reads as no other launch in the window carrying it. The fee recipient has a second floor, {recipient_floor} deployers or more, because the same recipient under one deployer is a person relaunching, and that is neither shown nor stored.
method.index.p: Per namespace, the first eight bytes of the hash of the normalized value as sixteen hex characters, and against it three fields: n, how many launches carry it; d, from how many distinct deployers; first, the UTC date of the earliest. The two skeleton namespaces add v, the number of distinct spellings in the group. No address, no raw string, no timestamp beyond a date.
viz.ticker.caption: {entries} tickers are carried by two launches or more. The busiest row is {mode} launches; the most carried ticker is on {max_n}, from {max_d} deployers.
viz.ticker.caption_tie: {entries} tickers are carried by two launches or more. The busiest row is {mode} launches; {max_ties} tickers tie at {max_n}.
viz.look.caption: Of {groups} ticker skeleton groups, {lookalike} hold spellings that differ as strings; the largest holds {largest}. Name skeletons yield {name_groups} such groups.
viz.link.caption: {entries} link values are carried by two launches or more. {single} of them come from a single deployer; the widest is carried by launches from {max_d} different deployers.
viz.link.caption_tie: {entries} link values are carried by two launches or more. {single} of them come from a single deployer; {max_ties} of them reach {max_d} different deployers.
faq.safe.q: Does this tell me if a launch is safe?
faq.safe.a: No. It tells you whether the strings a launch publishes are shared with other launches of one day, how many, from how many deployers, and since when. Whether a launch is safe, honest or worth anything is not something strings can say, and this page does not say it.
faq.copy.q: Does a shared ticker mean a launch is a copy?
faq.copy.a: No. It means the string is written by more than one launch in the window. The same ticker means one thing when a team relaunches under it and another when strangers converge on it, which is why the deployer count sits in the sentence and is never shown apart from it.
faq.day.a: A day is what one pass over the launch log covers at a pace the public endpoint sustains without a key. It is stated on the page with its block range and timestamps, and it is rebuilt every week. A longer window would say more about strings and nothing more about launches.
faq.hashes.q: Why hashes instead of the strings themselves?
faq.hashes.a: The index holds the first eight bytes of the hash of each normalized value with a count against it. That is enough to answer whether a value recurs and how widely, and it means the shipped file is not a directory of names, links and addresses.
faq.desc.q: Why is my description not compared?
faq.desc.a: Under {min_words} words after normalization, a description is too short to compare: short texts collide by coincidence and the count would say nothing. The check reports that it did not run rather than returning a figure it cannot stand behind.
faq.input.a: No. What you paste stays in your browser, and the comparison runs there against the table it fetched. Nothing is stored and no cookie is set. The page does make one request: the first time you check, it fetches that table from this domain, and nothing after that.
faq.code.a: Yes. The engine, the collector, the index writer, the tests and this page are in the repository linked in the footer. The engine is written in lintcha and copied here unchanged; a table in the repository names every copied file with its hash.
faq.who.a: The same person who runs lintcha, linked above. This site is not affiliated with Robinhood, pons or any launchpad, and it uses none of their marks.
faq.score.a: A score would need a model, a calibration and a public record of how often it was right. This site has none of those and is not building them. It reports what the strings share and stops, because a number that looks like a judgment would be read as one.
not.scanner.d: it does not read the contract, the bytecode or the state
not.score.d: no probability, no rating, no ordering, no colour that means good or bad
not.signal.d: a shared string is a fact about text, not a view on a launch
not.wallet.d: it holds no key, signs nothing, and cannot spend
not.feed.d: one day, rebuilt weekly, and the window is stated
not.affiliated.d: with Robinhood, pons or any launchpad
lore.kicker: Where the name, the mark and the window came from
lore.name.p: A linter reads a file and reports what is wrong with it without deciding whether the file is good. lintcha is a linter pointed at charters: the text an AI bot publishes about what it is, what it will do and what it will not touch. The name is those two words pushed together, and it stayed because nothing better turned up. This second site keeps it, because a launch is a charter too. A name, a ticker, a description and a few links, written once in the minute before a token exists and never read again by anyone.
lore.mark.p: The mark is a caret with two strokes cut out of it. A caret is the character an editor puts under the exact spot where something went wrong, which is the whole job in one symbol: point at the place, say nothing about the person. It is acid on near black because a linter has to be legible in a row of tabs, and because the colour belongs to the site and to nothing on the page that carries meaning. Green here is never a verdict.
lore.day.p: A day is the unit this page can show whole: one pass over the launch log, every launch in it, nothing sampled. It is not the window we would pick if the endpoint were faster, and it is the window we can stand behind without a key, without a private feed and without asking anyone for permission. A longer window would say more about strings and nothing more about launches. When the endpoint sustains more, the page will say so and show the new range, not quietly widen and hope nobody checks the block numbers.
lore.number.t: the number that is not here
lore.number.p: Every other tool on this chain ends in a figure: a score, a grade, a probability. That figure is the product, and it is also the part nobody can check, because it needs a model, a calibration and a public record of how often it was right. This page has none of those and is not building them. It says what is shared, with how many launches, from how many deployers, and since when, in a sentence, and then it stops. A count that looks like a judgement will be read as one, so there is no count that looks like one.
lore.token.p: $LINTCHA exists on the chain this page reads, which is the only reason it exists at all. It carries no revenue share, no fee cut, no vote and no claim on anything here. It cannot gate the code either: this repository is MIT, and the first fork would delete a paywall placed inside it. What it does is pay for the endpoint, the hosting and the hours, and it buys its holders a room and a bot, never an earlier reading or a better one.
lore.site.p: Everything on this page is something the repository already does, served so that nobody has to install anything to look. No wallet, nothing to sign, no account. Under the tool sits the command that prints the same result on your own machine, and beside it the hash of the file the page was built from. The site is a convenience, not the source: if it ever computes something the repository cannot, the repository has become decoration and the site has become a claim.

road.intro: lintcha reads what a launch wrote about itself and says what those strings are shared with. It runs in a browser, over an index anyone can rebuild, and it makes no claim about any launch. Here is what gets built next, in order, and what will not get built at all. No dates.
road.window.t: the window is the weakest part
road.window.p1: The index is rebuilt once a week. On the morning it runs, the window on this page is a few hours old. By the end of that week it is six days old, and nothing on the page tells you which of those two you are looking at. The block range and the timestamps are printed, so the information is there, but printing a number and telling someone what it means are different things, and we have been doing the first one.
road.window.p2: A count from a stale window is not wrong. It is a true statement about a day that has ended, and the page says which day. But somebody pasting a launch that happened this morning is comparing it with a set that does not contain this morning, and the sentence they read does not warn them. That is the gap, and it is ours, not the endpoint's.
road.window.p3: What goes in: the age of the window, in words, next to the result, so the reading carries its own staleness. Then a shorter gap between rebuilds, as often as the public endpoint sustains without a key. The window will not be widened to make the counts look bigger, and the refresh will not be moved to a quieter hour to make the run look cleaner. If a rebuild fails, the page keeps the old window and says the date, rather than showing a partial one.
road.room.p: A room on Telegram, and one bot in it. The bot posts every buy of the token as it clears the pool, answers the price and the contract to anyone who asks, and opens a holder check in a direct message for those who want one. It never messages anyone first, never asks for a key, a seed or an approval, and never holds funds. The holder check is a signature over a plain sentence that says in words that it moves nothing. Everything the bot says is read from the chain, and its code ships in this repository with the rest.
road.token.p: Creator fees from trading go to one wallet, and that wallet pays for the endpoint plan, the box the bot runs on and the hours that go into the index. There is nothing else attached: no share, no cut, no vote. What the token cannot do is more interesting than what it can. It cannot gate the code, because the licence is MIT. It cannot buy an earlier reading, because there is only one index and it is published. It cannot buy a better one, because a sharper private version would mean the public one is worse on purpose.
road.never.l1: no score, no probability, no rating, no ordering, and no colour that means good or bad
road.never.l2: no private index and no paid tier that reads more than this page reads
road.never.l3: no hosted key, and no signature anywhere that moves, approves or spends anything
road.never.l4: no third-party script, font, image, analytics or beacon on this site, on any page, ever
road.never.l5: no figure we did not read ourselves; a tile that cannot be read shows a dash and not a number from somewhere else
road.never.l6: no dates on this page, because a date that cannot be kept is worth less than a line that can be checked
road.never.l7: no closed core: if the site computes something the repository cannot, the repository is decoration
road.check.p: Commits show what shipped and when. The hash of the shipped index is printed above the command that rebuilds it, so anyone can run the command and compare. The vendor table names every file copied from lintcha with its hash, and a test recomputes all of them on every push. If something here goes quiet for weeks, ask about it in public.
token.p1: $LINTCHA is a token on this chain and nothing on this page depends on it. The page reads strings whether you hold it or not, and holding it buys no extra check and no private index. A holder can ask the bot to watch the log and write when a string they named appears; the check it runs is the one on this page, and the index it reads is the one published here.
